name: Naproxen
summary: A longer-acting NSAID often chosen when sustained coverage is desired and a relatively steadier cardiovascular profile is valued.
good: Longer-lasting pain control when twice-daily coverage is helpful.
bad: Patients with significant ulcer risk or impaired kidney reserve.
clinicalPearls: When a longer NSAID window is useful, naproxen is often the practical choice — but it is not GI-protective.
mechanism: Nonselective reversible COX inhibition with longer duration than ibuprofen.
indications: Dysmenorrhea, musculoskeletal pain, gout flares, and longer daytime coverage for inflammatory pain.
interactionNotes: Anticoagulants, corticosteroids, SSRIs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and diuretics all raise caution.

warnings: GI bleeding, renal injury, fluid retention, and late-pregnancy exposure remain important concerns.

Nonselective; some data suggest more balanced/sustained COX-1 inhibition than diclofenac, partly explaining its comparatively favorable CV signal.
Comparable to or somewhat higher than ibuprofen at equivalent anti-inflammatory doses.
Among the lower CV-risk options within the nonselective NSAID group in observational and meta-analytic data — though not risk-free.
Same class-level mechanism as other nonselective NSAIDs.
